title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). Generation used gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed end‑to‑end acceptance checks (syntactic, ordering/dependency, and final‑state constraints). Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with a single shared LLM generation per pair (model_calls_used = 120). Deterministic scoring yielded contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (both arms accepted the shared candidates for all pairs). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because the run intentionally shared each LLM candidate across arms, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates and do not exercise independent generator variance or repair coverage. We add an explicit evidence‑to‑claim mapping, a compact nearest‑work comparison, per‑task validator trace exemplars, execution accounting, and reproducibility guidance grounded in archived artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical. Correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, and no transient safety violations) are required while preserving flexibility for expressive operator intents across vendor CLIs. Two architectural paradigms are widely discussed in research and engineering practice: (i) translation‑first architectures that constrain generation into a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solver synthesis to ensure deterministic device guarantees, and (ii) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators and bounded repair/rollback to achieve correctness while preserving generator flexibility.

This study tested a narrowly specified, preregistered question under an explicit design choice: given identical LLM candidate configurations for each task pair, do downstream translation‑first and agentic orchestration paths differ in deterministic validator acceptance? The preregistered confirmatory estimand therefore measured validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics, not independent generator or repair performance. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment using synthetic intent tasks and deterministic validation that precisely quantifies validator‑acceptance parity under shared candidate semantics; (2) a compact evidence‑to‑claim table that maps each preregistered hypothesis/estimand to archived artifacts and declares whether it was tested or unobserved; (3) a nearest‑work comparison matrix situating this run relative to representative translation→verify and LLM‑agent NetOps studies; and (4) concrete, artifact‑grounded protocol modifications and reproducibility advice required to convert this validator‑parity test into a discriminating independent‑generator/repair head‑to‑head comparison.
sections.related_work:
Two research traditions frame our positioning. First, formal translation→verification literature emphasizes constrained synthesis and deterministic guarantees for network configurations (foundational verification/synthesis work and extensions to quantitative verification). Representative formal works emphasize soundness and solver‑guided synthesis where generator variance is not the central variable. Second, LLM‑driven NetOps and agentic AIOps research focuses on flexible generation, tool orchestration, and iterative repair; these works stress deterministic validators and bounded self‑correction as necessary to bound hallucination and unsafe proposals.

Nearest‑work comparison (compact). We compare three representative studies on four experimental axes: independent generation sampling, repair loop instrumentation, validator‑acceptance focus, and emulator/hardware realism.
• INTA (ICNP 2025) [3]: independent LLM generation sampling = yes; repair loops = limited; validator acceptance = partial; emulator = Mininet‑derived.
• Mahmood & Song (IFIP Networking 2026) [4]: independent generation = yes; active multi‑agent repair loops = yes; validator acceptance = emphasized; domain = Kubernetes network policies.
• Weighted NetKAT and formal verification literature [5,10–12]: independent generation = not applicable (formal synthesis); repair loops = solver‑based; validator acceptance = core; emulator = verification models.

Distinction of the present run. Unlike the above, our preregistered shared_candidate design holds the generator output constant across arms and therefore isolates validator acceptance. This produces a narrow but precise confirmatory measurement: validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than an adjudication of generator or repair robustness. The evidence supporting this characterization is archived (execution manifest, per‑task validator traces, and analysis artifacts).
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. The study preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed: primary estimand = paired difference in binary end‑to‑end correctness (A − B), confirmatory N = 120 paired tasks, declared generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 (bootstrap percentile CIs and exact McNemar) was preregistered; bootstrap parameters were 10,000 resamples with seed 1729.

Task generation and constraints. Tasks were produced by a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Each task manifest entry contains: intent text; initial/final expected states; a required safe sequence (explicit command order constraints such as shutdown→modify→restore or make‑before‑break switchover); difficulty metadata (levels: medium/hard/very_hard); and a canonical reference answer. Representative task manifests and their canonical reference answers are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl and representative task files such as task‑000001 manifest excerpt).

Orchestration and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The adapter implemented shared_initial_candidate: for each paired task the orchestration performed a single LLM call (shared candidate) which was then provided identically to both downstream arms (translation‑first and agentic). Execution accounting shows planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false, demonstrating per‑call isolation and adherence to contamination controls.

Validator rules, scoring mechanics, and decision logic. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5 v5.0) applied the preregistered full_intent_constraint_validation rule set: normalization, required command inclusion, ordering and dependency checks (e.g., ensure make‑before‑break when required), final‑state consistency with expected_state, and an overall boolean validation_after.valid that defines pass/fail for end‑to‑end correctness. Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record normalized_response, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, validation_before/after snapshots, and repair_applied flags. A configuration is scored 1 (pass) only when validation_after.valid == true.

Statistical analysis executor. Analysis used the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. Primary outputs: paired contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), paired difference A − B, bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729), and exact McNemar two‑sided test. Secondary estimands (repair coverage and repair iterations) and subgroup analyses were preregistered but contingent on observing repair events.

sections.discussion:
What this run measures — and what it does not. By design (preregistered and executed), the run isolates validator‑acceptance parity: for identical LLM candidate configurations provided to both orchestration arms, do the translation‑first and agentic validators differ in acceptance? The observed degenerate concordance (n11 = 120) answers this restricted question: both validators accepted the identical candidates for every paired task. This outcome does not imply equivalence of architectures under independent generation or repair because generator variance and repair loops were not exercised.

Evidence‑to‑claim table (compact, artifact‑grounded). Each preregistered hypothesis/estimand is mapped to the measured quantity and archived artifacts:
1) H1 (Paired difference A − B in end‑to‑end correctness): Measured estimand in this run = validator‑acceptance parity under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Supporting artifacts: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini), execution/execution_manifest.json. Status: tested (measured estimand narrower than originally phrased in the high‑level preregistration).
2) H2 (Agentic pipeline repair coverage > translation‑first): Measured? No — repair_applied = false in execution/scoring/*.json. Supporting artifacts: execution/scoring/*.json (repair_applied flags) and analysis/missingness_summary.csv. Status: unobserved (secondary estimand not instantiated).
3) Secondary subgroup analyses and multiplicity adjustments: No discordant outcomes to analyze; supporting artifacts: analysis/* CSVs. Status: uninformative for this execution.

Why repairs were not observed. The synthetic task generator's calibration and the validator rule set produced many tasks whose canonical reference answers matched the shared LLM candidates after normalization; thus validators accepted candidates without invoking the repair path. The archived scoring JSONs document repair_applied=false per episode. This is an empirical property of the chosen task bank and shared candidate semantics rather than of the repair machinery itself.

Protocol modifications to obtain a discriminating head‑to‑head comparison (artifact‑grounded). The manifest shows the execution bookkeeping that will change if the preregistered design is modified: (i) remove shared_initial_candidate so each arm receives an independent LLM generation per pair — model_calls_used would increase to 240 initial calls; (ii) allow multiple sampled generations per arm to estimate generator variance (further increasing model_calls and enabling generator‑level estimands); (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations (repair_applied counters and repair trace artifacts expected to become nonzero); (iv) increase emulator fidelity or include hardware to reduce simulator/hardware contamination risk. Each of these modifications is already supported in the preregistration machinery and would reflect deterministically in execution artifacts (model_calls_used, provider_call_audit counts, nonzero repair_applied flags).

Operational implications. The run documents a practical use case: archived shared‑candidate experiments can serve as a regression test for validator equivalence and orchestrator decision‑parity. For organizations comparing validators or migrating verifier implementations, a shared‑candidate, artifactized acceptance test suite provides repeatable, low‑variance assessments. However, production decisions about which architecture yields superior independent generation or repair coverage require follow‑up experiments that exercise generator sampling and repair loops as described above.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted the identical shared candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false for all episodes); preregistered hypotheses about repair coverage were therefore unobserved. The run demonstrates a reproducible protocol for validator‑acceptance parity testing and documents the precise artifact changes required to evolve the protocol into a discriminating independent‑generator/repair head‑to‑head comparison. All execution, scoring, and analysis artifacts supporting these claims are archived and referenced in the execution manifest and analysis artifacts included with this submission.

limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation or repair robustness differences between architectures.
The task corpus was synthetic and executed in Mininet‑derived emulation; emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single declared LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric operationalizes correctness per validator rules but does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust.
